Faber 1.14.0

FieldValue
ProductFaber
Version1.14.0
LicenseMIT

Install this version#

No prebuilt archives were published for this version. It is listed here because its release notes are part of the record.

Release notes#

Status: final — tagged faber/v1.14.0 on 2026-10-16

Faber 1.14 is the first release after the source went public. Programs can now touch the outside world: the file system, console, process, clock and entropy modules run under faber run and in generated Rust, and their failures are values with a kind and a path. The language gets typed holes and open records, an insertion-ordered ledger map, tighter escapes and templates, bytes as list<b8>, and checked axis markers on tensor row operations. Several of these are breaking changes; read that section before you upgrade.

Language#

Failures are values. The standard library reports failure as ⇥ IoFault, a union with one variant per kind of failure (NotFound, Permission, ConnectionRefused, TimedOut, and so on). A variant carries the path or address the program passed and no message text; platform text appears only in debug output. A caught fault prints as IoFault.NotFound { path = "/nonexistent/x" } on the runner and in generated Rust alike. Absence is not a failure: the end of input and an unset variable are ∪ none.

Holes and open records. A typed cell can solve its own holes: list<_>[1, 2] solves the element type, tuple<_, string>[1, "x"] solves one slot, and a bare [..] or _ [..] into a set cell builds the set. record<*> declares a record whose whole field list is left to inference, and a bare { field = value } literal with no cell to name it is such a record. (record<g: f32, *>, a partial list with a hole, is PARSE001 ratio_field_list_hole_not_sole.) An untyped empty literal, {} or [] with nothing to name its type, is a named error. The stated keyed constructor Type { "k": v } builds JSON and map<K, V> values.

main {
    let list<int> xs ← list<_>[1, 2]
    let tuple<int, string> pair ← tuple<_, string>[1, "x"]
    let set<int> seen ← [1, 2, 2]
    print xs.length(), seen.length()
    print "§0 and §0 and §1"("a", "b")
    print «say "hi"»
    print pair
}
2 2
a and a and b
say "hi"
tuple [1, "x"]

Ledger. ledger<K, V> is an insertion-ordered map. The runner constructs it from a keyed literal, indexes, stores, deletes, counts, tests membership, loops in insertion order, compares (order matters for ≡), and prints it. Conversions, sort and the other wrapper operations are refused by name (SEM010 ledger_operation_not_implemented). Every other target refuses the type (CODEGEN001 ledger_type_unsupported_on_target).

main {
    mut ledger<string, int> tally ← { "b": 2, "a": 1 }
    tally["c"] ← 3
    tally["a"] ← 10
    for from tally at [name] let count {
        print name, count
    }
    print tally.length()
}
b 2
a 10
c 3
3

Bytes are `list<b8>`. list<b8> and the bounded list<b8, N> are the byte types in the standard library, the corpus, the re-emitter and the grammar; faber format rewrites the older byte-string spellings to them. The scalar words byte and byte are retired (SEM008 retired_byte_word): write b8 for raw bits or u8 for a number. Converting a list to a bounded list checks the length and reports a recoverable failure. Converting a sized number to a bounded byte list is n ↦ list<b8, 4> via Le (or via Be), bit-exact on the runner and in generated Rust; the other targets refuse the row by name. x ↦ f32 rounds to binary32, and so does storing a float into a bare f32 local on the runner.

Text and escapes. A string literal may escape only its own delimiter, the backslash, n, t, r and u{…}; any other escape is LEX003 unknown_escape. A string that contains quotes can use guillemets, «say "hi"», with no escapes, and the lint WARN034 suggests that rewrite. Regex literals (regex /pattern/, or _ /pattern/ where the type is known) keep their body raw and round-trip through faber format. The pattern is not checked by faber check: an invalid one fails when the program runs.

Templates. A numbered hole §N selects argument N, counting from 0, and may repeat; a repeated hole evaluates its argument once on every target that supports templates. Every position from §0 up to the highest hole must be read: a gap in the numbering is SEM008 template_hole_index_gap, and an argument that no hole reads is SEM008 template_application_arity_mismatch.

Instants. ≅ and ≇ compare instants of different precisions.

Range containment. x ∈ 1‥5 and x ∉ 1‥5 now run on the runner and emit on every target except Haskell, which still refuses ranges.

Tensor row operations. sum, mean and softmax take the axis marker at the call: t.sum(axis 1), t.sum(axis 1, axis 2), or a named constant, t.sum(axis K). softmax takes an optional axis and only the last axis is legal (SEM010 softmax_axis_not_last). norm_rms and norm_layer require the marker too, as in input.norm_rms(axis 1, 1e-5, weight). rope_half and softmax_causal are source methods.

Diagnostics. The six translated reader packs (ar, hi, th-TH, vi, zh-Hans, zh-Hant) now translate the rows that used to repeat the English text, and the parser's "expected X" errors carry named issues instead of prose. New codes include LEX003 unknown_escape, WARN034, SEM008 template_hole_index_gap and PKG001 target_not_in_this_build.

Tooling#

Compiled programs can do I/O. The standard library's file-system, console, process, clock and entropy modules run through native leaves, both under faber run and in a Rust package built with faber build --target rust; TCP, an HTTP client and a WebSocket client run under faber run. The 1.13 gate that stopped such builds (PKG001 package_host_selection_required) no longer fires for these modules. time.now() works under faber run. Text, encoding, TOML, digests and HMAC are ordinary Faber. No standard-library function is marked deferred any more, and the stub modules cache, compression, database, model, optimizer and yaml are deleted. The limits of this route are under Known issues.

Library location. --library-home <dir> on the command line and [paths] library_home in faber.toml select where optional libraries are found; the standard library is embedded and needs neither. The FABER_LIBRARY_HOME environment variable is ignored, and so are the other FABER_* and RADIX_* variables that used to change behaviour (cache home, support-path override, shuffle seed, Metal and device debug switches, the TLA checker paths); each has a flag or a manifest key. There is still no package manager or library install command.

New and changed flags. faber run --shuffle-seed N, faber run --debug, faber run --threads N, faber test --solum-in NAME, faber corpus --filter TEXT, and radix verify --tla-jar PATH --java-bin PATH. --threads is accepted only with --device cpu, and until the worker device lands it has no effect (faber prints a note saying so). The corpus runner reports a rejects outcome for programs that are meant to be refused, and timeout_secs now bounds only the run phase; setup phases have their own bound.

Generated code spells names differently. Parameters and locals are emitted with p_ and l_ prefixes in Rust, Go, TypeScript, Swift, Python and Haskell so that a Faber name can never collide with a target keyword; device kernels are k<id> and their buffers b<N>. Regenerate generated code; older output and this release's runtimes do not mix.

Targets. Go gets lazy generators (a range-over-function iterator), imported generators, and package builds that emit declarations from sibling modules; Go and TypeScript use the exporter's canonical spelling for imported names. Swift emits @escaping where needed, copies owned collection and class parameters on entry, and imports Darwin or Glibc by platform. Python gets maps, sets and set operations. TypeScript bounded lists are native arrays with a length check. WebAssembly lowers scalar sqrt inline and handles recovered float-to-integer conversions. The Go runtime library gains stdio, process, clock and entropy leaves, which faber build --target go does not use yet. Metal and WGSL max and min reductions seed from element 0.

`PKG001 target_not_in_this_build`. Asking a build for a target it was compiled without now answers PKG001 target_not_in_this_build instead of failing later. The released binary carries Rust, Faber, TypeScript, Go, Swift, Python, Haskell, FHIR, FMIR, WebAssembly, LLVM, Metal, WGSL and S-expression emitters. It also carries two preview targets. -t c writes readable C from a checked program, rejects constructs it cannot express by name, and builds with GCC or Clang. -t clif writes a native object through Cranelift for a fail-closed subset, and faber build --target clif links it. The experimental Pascal, COBOL, Fortran, Odin and BASIC targets are not part of the binary.

GPU#

faber run --device cpu and --device metal run @ kernel functions; the Metal route works on Apple silicon (a two-element kernel gave the same result on both). In this release the device gate admits class locals (constructed, read and written) inside lane-form kernels, Metal lowers elementwise add, subtract, multiply and negate in a kernel, a rank-1 right operand is admitted for matmul, and the max and min reductions on Metal and WGSL seed correctly. --device reference runs a kernel as plain sequential code on the runner, the oracle that device results are compared with. CPU, FMIR and runner timings are not GPU performance; no GPU throughput claim is made here.

Breaking changes#

  1. Binding words. Four words now say how a name is bound.
WordMeaningLatin
let T x ← ea fixed namelet
mut T x ← ere-pointable and writablemut
ref T x ← ere-pointable and read-onlyref
const T X = ea compile-time fact, set with =const

Rewrite old code by this table: a run-time const T x ← e becomes let T x ← e, and var T x ← e becomes mut T x ← e. A compile-time const T X = e stays as it is. The old spellings are errors: var is PARSE010 var_retired, and a run-time const T x ← e (Latin const) is PARSE010 runtime_const_retired. The product does not ship a migration tool, and faber format refuses a file that still holds the old words, so run faber check, which names every site, and rewrite by hand. A bare parameter is ref: the function may read it and may not write it. To write a parameter, mark it mut in the signature and at the call, grow(mut xs). A ref or mut name may hold T ∪ none when the other member is a reference type (a class, a collection or text). Over a number or other scalar it is SEM008 scalar_access_marker, bare or optional. The binders of a loop, from, match, sort, reduce and destructuring take let or mut. A const binder is PARSE010 binder_fixum_retired, and a ref binder is PARSE010 ref_binder_refused.

   class Node {
       const int LIMIT = 3
       let string tag = "n"
       mut int value
       mut Node next optional
   }

   fn grow(mut list<int> xs) → void {
       xs.append(9)
   }

   fn last(Node head) → int {
       ref Node ∪ none cursor ← head
       while cursor not is none {
           if cursor.next is none {
               return cursor.value
           }
           cursor ← cursor.next
       }
       return head.value
   }

   main {
       let Node b ← Node { value = 2 }
       let Node a ← Node { value = 1, next = b }
       mut list<int> xs ← [1]
       grow(mut xs)
       print last(a), Node.LIMIT, xs.length()
   }
   2 3 2
  1. Class fields. An instance field is let T x = e (fixed after construction) or mut T x = e (writable). A field marked ref is PARSE010 ref_field_refused. The old read-only field const T x with no initializer is PARSE010 const_member_requires_initializer, and var T x is PARSE010 field_modifier_missing; write let and mut. A field written const T X = e is now a type-level constant, not an instance field (see the next entry).
  2. Class-level `static` members. static (Latin static) members of a class are retired: static T X = e there is PARSE010 static_member_retired. A type-level constant is const T X = e in the class body, and you read it through the type, Tab.X. Storing into it is SEM020 assignment_to_const_member. State that changes belongs in a mut field.
  3. Environment variables. FABER_LIBRARY_HOME and the other FABER_* and RADIX_* switches listed under Tooling no longer do anything; use --library-home, [paths] library_home and the new flags.
  4. Unknown escapes. An unknown backslash escape in a string literal is LEX003 unknown_escape; the old pass-through is gone. Use a guillemet string for text with quotes.
  5. Empty literals. {} and [] need a typed cell (a declared type or an inference site); let a ← {} is SEM016 inferred_constructor_no_expected_type and let list<_> a ← [] is SEM014 cannot_infer_empty_list_element_type.
  6. Templates. Numbered holes count from 0; a template that skips a number or leaves an argument unread is now an error.
  7. Row operations need the axis marker. norm_rms(1, …) and norm_layer(1, …) with a bare integer are SEM057 axis_marker_required; write axis 1. sum(1) and mean(1) with a bare integer are unknown methods.
  8. Renamed methods. rms_norm is norm_rms, rope_norm is norm_rope, layer_norm is norm_layer; the Vector, Matrix and Tensor elementwise methods are subtracted, multiplied and divided (the old subtract, multiply and divide on those types are unknown methods); the set method symmetric_difference is difference_symmetric, and the sparse nonzero_count is count_nonzero.
  9. Standard library signatures. File-system, process, console, net, HTTP and WebSocket calls report ⇥ IoFault; end of input (console.read_line, console.read_bytes) and an unset variable (process.read_env) are ∪ none. process.spawn and process.detach no longer take directory and environment. time.interval returns a Ticker that you read with time.tick. Callers that matched on the old error types must be updated.
  10. Removed library modules. norma:cache, norma:compression, norma:database, norma:model, norma:optimizer and norma:yaml are gone; importing one is PKG001 unknown_library_module.
  11. Generated identifiers. Emitted names carry p_ and l_ prefixes (see Tooling); anything that scraped generated source must follow.

Known issues#

Carried from 1.13 and re-checked against this build. Two 1.13 items are fixed (range containment on the MIR targets, and faber convert on files that import library types), and compiled programs can now do I/O, with the edges listed first below.

  • Libraries cannot be installed. The graphics, autograd and UI libraries still have no install command and faber doctor reports them not found; --library-home only points at a directory.
  • The I/O route has edges.
  • Under faber run, the *_async file, clock and TCP wrappers are refused during lowering, an HTTP server and client in one program (a loopback) is refused, and a WebSocket client and server in one program can hang instead of finishing.
  • In generated Rust, a package that uses TCP, HTTP or WebSocket does not compile (faber build --target rust hands rustc a program it rejects), and a few catch forms over an imported IoFault do not compile either.
  • Go and TypeScript packages build for pure code, but a package that uses the I/O modules is refused (PKG001 leaf_unsupported_on_target for Go; the TypeScript build fails in code generation). faber targets still lists Go and TypeScript package compilation as unsupported even though pure-code packages build.
  • Records without a declared type do not run. A bare { field = value } literal checks and emits in Rust, but the runner stops with missing type information for MIR lowering; write record<g: f32, w: int> { g = 1.0, w = 2 } to run one.
  • Printing a `list<b8, N>` on the runner writes the raw bytes instead of [0x01, 0x02, …]; an unbounded list<b8> prints correctly.
  • Some shipped example files are stale. Most of the loose example files under the standard library's exempla directory (the chorda and stdlib-nativum groups) fail faber check because they import module names that no longer exist, such as norma:solum; three more fail on tensor calls or a missing export. The example packages there check clean.
  • Device limits. The full-size flood simulation completes on Metal, but its accuracy comparison against the donor program was withdrawn because no correct run can meet it; the reduced grid is still checked to 0.01 m. A throwing kernel can throw only a constant text per failure site. The CPU worker count has no effect yet.
  • Regex engine gaps by target (carried): Go has no Unicode \b; TypeScript, Swift and Python differ from the dialect on named constructs and the backtracking engines can take exponential time on hostile patterns; Racket (sexp) and Haskell refuse every regex construct.
  • Haskell also refuses string templates and ranges.
  • WebAssembly types a 32-bit float local as f64.
  • Ledger runs only on the runner, and ledger<K, V> {} with an empty brace body is refused as an unfinished operation; use a keyed literal.

Not in this release#

  • A package manager and library install command. Cista has no published release.
  • Ratio, plus-minus and superscript-power types and the set-algebra glyphs are designed but not built (x², ± and ∖ are lexical errors).
  • trap { } still returns a bare union of its result and error types. The built-in trapped<R, T> result type is registered in the compiler, but its name cannot be written in source yet.
  • The C and Cranelift targets are previews: they cover a subset of the language and refuse the rest by name. Neither runs under faber run.
  • The CUDA backend exists behind hardware-gated checks; no CUDA route is enabled for faber run.
  • Radix stays at 0.84.0 (no separate Radix release).
  • Public publication of the Go runtime module and @faber/runtime is still pending; neither is on its package registry.

Open source#

Faber's source is public at <https://github.com/faberlang/faber> under MIT OR Apache-2.0. The repository holds the compiler front end, the reference runner, the standard library (Norma), the grammar and locale packs, the corpus and a public test suite, the FHIR artifact seam and the C generator, and it builds a working faber that checks, formats and runs programs. The released binary also carries the code generators that are not part of the public source (Rust, Go, TypeScript, Swift, Python, Haskell, LLVM, WebAssembly and the GPU emitters), which is why installing this release, not building the public tree, is the way to get every target. The repository takes no outside pull requests.

The previous public repository is now faberlang/faber-1.x and is archived. Its v1.x tags were carried into the new repository, so projects pinned to a 1.x tag keep resolving. History in the new repository starts on 2026-08-02. Releases continue to be published at <https://github.com/faberlang/releases>.
